summary:
Chris Noring opens by polling the audience, confirming most have shifted from pure coding to a systems approach. He frames the old model: developers were the bottleneck, producing 100% of code linearly, forced to prioritize features. That limitation is gone. The new reality is that developers still have jobs, but their center of gravity moved; they write code selectively, aided by AI tools. He acknowledges the AI slope problem—early AI-generated code created more cleanup work—but says guardrails now define the developer experience.

He proposes a three-stage workflow: start in the CLI (GitHub Copilot CLI or equivalent), use the editor as a familiar control board for fine adjustments, and scale through agents in the CLI or GitHub UI. The CLI becomes the entry point for drafting, managing issues and PRs, and issuing prompts. The editor remains valuable but occupies less time as agents multiply.

The core problem is that without rules, agents run amok. His first guardrail is agents.md, a bare-minimum file in every repo explaining repository intent, architecture, constraints, dos and don'ts, and agent responsibilities. A second guardrail is skills: repeatable, constrained contracts agents invoke instead of improvising, each living in its own folder with a skill.md. Skills can be invoked via slash commands or by typing a prompt resembling the skill name or description.

The third guardrail is custom agents, needed when skills are insufficient. A custom agent is a higher-level concept with a persona, a distinct role and purpose (e.g., security expert, back-ender, front-ender), the ability to use n number of skills, and access to MCP servers. Agents are orchestrators—broader in scope, able to plan and reason. Custom agent files live in .github/agents and must be called .agent. Their front matter includes argument hints and tools, which constrain what the agent can do (e.g., read, search the web, create to-do lists). A researcher agent, for instance, is constrained to web work and cannot create or edit files.

The scaling chapter shows delegation in action. From the CLI, calling /delegate sends a session to GitHub, which starts a job and creates a draft PR. Agents work in sandboxes and cannot break out, but they can create PRs, bringing humans into the loop as reviewers. From the GitHub UI, users assign agents to issues, each becoming a feature or bug fix. Copilot processes the assignment, shows work-in-progress status, and returns a draft PR for review. Noring compares this era to moving from axes to chainsaws. He calls agents toddlers—sometimes genius, sometimes dumb—underscoring the need for a harness. The closing message: AI amplifies developers rather than replacing them, and the industry still wants engineering brains.

takeaways: The developer role has shifted from being the linear code-producing bottleneck to system designer, planner, and agent orchestrator.
Three guardrails prevent AI-assisted fragmentation: agents.md (repo intent and constraints), skills (repeatable contracts), and custom agents (orchestrators with personas, tools, and MCP access).
Custom agents are higher-level than skills—they can plan, reason, use multiple skills, access MCP servers, and are constrained via tools in their front matter.
Scaling happens via /delegate in the CLI or assigning agents to issues in the GitHub UI; agents work in sandboxes and produce draft PRs for human review.
Human-in-the-loop approval gates remain essential; humans review draft PRs and can still be the ones who merge.
Agents behave unpredictably—sometimes genius, sometimes dumb—likened to toddlers, requiring a harness of guardrails.
The editor is used less for implementation and more for fine adjustments as agents handle larger implementation work.
AI amplifies developers rather than replacing them; the industry still wants engineering brains.
Understand the shift from code producer to system designer and agent orchestrator
Learn to establish agents.md as a high-level guardrail in repositories

sections.title: Introduction and Audience Polling
sections.summary: Chris introduces himself, polls the audience on coding habits and tool usage, and notes roughly half use Claude and half use Copilot.

sections.title: The Shifting Developer Role
sections.summary: Describes the old model where developers were the linear bottleneck and the new reality where the center of gravity has moved to system design with AI helpers.

sections.title: Proposed CLI-First Workflow
sections.summary: Proposes starting in the CLI for drafting and issue management, using the editor as a control board, and scaling through agents in CLI or GitHub UI.

sections.title: Guardrail One: agents.md
sections.summary: Introduces agents.md as the bare-minimum guardrail encoding repo intent, architecture, constraints, and agent responsibilities, demonstrated with a finance tracker repo.

sections.title: Guardrail Two: Skills
sections.summary: Introduces skills as constrained repeatable contracts agents invoke, explains folder structure with skill.md, and shows asking Copilot for help writing better instructions.

sections.title: Guardrail Three: Custom Agents
sections.summary: Introduces custom agents as the next level above skills—orchestrators with personas, tools, MCP access, reasoning and planning ability. Explains file placement in .github/agents, front matter with argument hints and tools constraints, and demos a researcher agent.

sections.title: Scaling Through Delegation
sections.summary: Shows scaling via /delegate in the CLI sending sessions to GitHub to create draft PRs, and assigning agents to issues in the GitHub UI. Agents work in sandboxes with human-in-the-loop review gates.

sections.title: Summary and Closing Message
sections.summary: Recaps the axes-to-chainsaw analogy, emphasizes guardrails (agents.md, skills, custom agents) as essential to avoid 20x slop, and delivers the closing message that AI amplifies developers rather than replacing them.
